newsitem.title: INDIA: India forex policy seen hurting growth - HSBC.
newsitem.headline: India forex policy seen hurting growth - HSBC.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) foreign exchange policy is damaging exports and retarding industrial growth, securities firm HSBC Batlivala & Karani said in a report on Tuesday.
"We believe the current policy of the RBI to maintain an appreciated rupee in real effective exchange rates (REER) is hurting exports and consequently industrial growth," it said.
The RBI, which does not publish an up to date REER index, has said the rupee rose five percent on the index in the year to December 1996.
Rajan Govil, HSBC economist and author of the report, said the rupee is now six percent higher on the index than December 1995.
"The higher REER also has the potential to directly retard industrial growth since it makes imports of competing products cheaper," the report said.
"We shall be downgrading our industrial growth forecast of 9.0 percent for FY1998 if we do not see the rupee depreciating to 36 against the dollar levels in the coming four to six weeks."
It said Indian exports have fallen by 4.6 percent year-on-year from November 1996 to April 1997 largely because of rupee's appreciation against major international currencies.
The Indian rupee has remained at 35.7-35.9 range against the dollar during the last 11 months, HSBC Batlivala & Karani said.
"The Indian rupee, at the same time, appreciated against all international currencies including those of export competing countries such as Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh."
This had hurt Indian export competitiveness, it said.
The overvalued rupee made imports cheaper.
"We believe the RBI should intervene in the forex market more aggressively to ensure the depreciation of the rupee in the immediate future," HSBC Batlivala & Karani said.

The rupee is expected to depreciate to 37.8 against the dollar by end March 1998, aided by a higher trade deficit and a deceleration in NRI (non-resident Indian) deposit growth with reimposition of SLR and CRR on these deposits," it said.
SLR refers to statutory liquidity ratio and CRR refers to cash reserve ratio for Indian banks.
